title: The system: a code-hosting platform's watch inbox
caption: One repository event is saved once, published to a log, and copied into the inbox of every watcher, except for the few very popular repos, which are merged in when the inbox is read.

steps.text: A developer pushes commits, opens an issue or cuts a release. The repo service saves the event and an outbox row in one transaction and answers right away: the developer never waits for watchers.
A relay publishes outbox rows to the event log, keyed by repository id, so one repo's events stay in order.
Fan-out workers read the event, page through the repo's watchers and append the event id to each watcher's inbox. Most repos have a handful of watchers, so this is a few small writes.
Above the watcher threshold (read from config) the worker skips the copies and writes the event once to the hot-repo recents.

A watcher opens the inbox: the API reads their id list, merges in recent events of the few popular repos they watch, then hydrates the page from the repo DB and drops anything deleted or no longer visible.
The digest worker is a second consumer of the same log. It collects events for people who chose email and sends one summary per hour or per day, without touching the inbox path.

scenarios.name: Popular repo release
scenarios.summary: A repo with 300 000 watchers ships a release: one write instead of 300 000, and readers pay a small merge instead.

steps.text: The release is saved and published like any other event.
The worker sees 300 000 watchers against a threshold of 10 000 and writes the event once to the hot-repo recents.
Each watcher who opens the inbox gets it merged in at read time. The recents are tiny and replicated, so the merge is a few cached reads.
Email still goes out, but in batches the email service can absorb, spread over the digest window.

scenarios.name: Fan-out worker crash
scenarios.summary: A worker dies half-way through an event's watchers. Nothing is lost and nothing is shown twice, because the offset and the inbox writes are both safe to replay.

steps.text: A worker crashes after writing 3 000 of an event's 8 000 inbox entries.
Its log offset was never committed, so another worker takes over the partition and reads the same event again.
It writes all 8 000 entries again. Entries are keyed by event id, so the 3 000 repeats overwrite themselves instead of appearing twice.
Watchers see the event a little late. An alert on consumer lag tells the on-call engineer if it happens often.

scenarios.name: Threshold lowered
scenarios.summary: Workers fall behind during a busy week: an operator lowers the threshold, and more repos move to read-time merge without a deploy.

steps.text: An operator lowers the watcher threshold from 10 000 to 5 000 in the config store.
Workers pick it up within seconds. Events from repos with 5 000 to 10 000 watchers now go to the recents instead of every inbox.
Entries already in inboxes stay. Readers now merge a few more repos, which is the cost of the cheaper writes.
